![](/static/diagrams/29-correcting-a-published-figure.png){fig-alt="Two cards split a revision, which is expected, from a correction, which is an error. Arrows run from the correction card to three grade cards: significant in red, minor but significant in yellow, minor and insignificant in green, each with what happens. A dark blue band names who decides. Everything is set out in the text below the picture."}

<details>
<summary>Text description of this diagram</summary>

**First: is it a revision or a correction?** They are not the same thing.

**A revision is expected.** Statistics published as provisional and later finalised, a change of
methodology, or the arrival of further data. Nothing on this page follows from it.

**A correction is an error.** The policy grades errors **by consequence rather than by size**. Which
of the three grades applies decides what has to happen and how quickly. Arrows run from this card to
each of the three.

| The error | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Significant**, where the change would contradict the conclusions previously drawn from the data | A prominent alert on the website, corrected as soon as possible, and communicated to users and stakeholders |
| **Minor but significant**, insubstantial but warranting immediate correction in professional judgement | The published release is amended and the revision is clearly identified in it |
| **Minor and insignificant**, where a correction would reasonably be deemed inconsequential | Corrected at the next scheduled release rather than immediately |

**Who decides, and what gets published.** Decisions on how to address an error in published
statistics are made by the **Lead Official for Statistics**, in consultation with the National
Statistician as appropriate, and the amendment is published alongside the link to the document. Where
an error is known but corrected figures are not yet available, a note goes on the statistics saying
so and making clear the figures are subject to change. [NHSBSA Revisions and Corrections Policy v002,
sections 2 and 3]

**If your output is not official statistics.** The policy binds official and national statistics. The
behaviour it describes is worth following anywhere: say what was wrong, say what it changed, say
where the corrected version is, and leave the original visible rather than replacing it silently. An
analysis that quietly acquires new numbers is indistinguishable from an analysis nobody checked.

**Where this connects.** A correction is a change to data, method or output after sign-off, so at
Level 3 the change control check applies and it is re-assured proportionately
([section 6](/guidance/06-doing-the-work/index.qmd)). What the correction shows about how the error got
through is a lesson, and [section 11](/guidance/11-review-and-continuous-improvement/index.qmd) is where it
goes. [Section 12](/guidance/12-tools-and-templates/index.qmd) lists the policy itself.

**The grading is by consequence rather than by size**, which is the part people get wrong: a small
arithmetic slip that reverses a conclusion is significant, and a large number restated without
changing anything anyone decided is not.

</details>
